title: Same breakout rules on four NQ candle sizes: the 5 minute version lost 99% and the 15 minute version made 147%
author: person-person12
selftext:
Everybody has an opinion about which timeframe to trade and almost nobody has run the same rules on more than one of them. I had one set of breakout rules sitting in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) and about 400,000 NQ candles, so I ran it four times and changed nothing but the candle size.

Identical code every run. Long when price closes above the highest high of the last 20 candles, short below the lowest low, 2x ATR stop and 2x ATR target, one contract, 100k account, January 2021 to the end of September 2026. Commission and slippage charged on both sides at $2.50 a contract plus half a tick.

* **5 minute: 11,183 trades, 50.1% wins, profit factor 0.98, net -99.2%**
* 15 minute: 3,936 trades, 52.0% wins, profit factor 1.06, net +147.0%
* 30 minute: 2,254 trades, 51.9% wins, profit factor 1.06, net +114.7%
* 1 hour: 1,130 trades, 52.3% wins, profit factor 1.03, net +34.6%

The win rates are 50.1, 52.0, 51.9 and 52.3. The rules read the market about equally well on all four candle sizes. What changed is how many times they paid to find out.

The 5 minute version made **+12.7% before costs** and handed over $111,830 in commission and slippage across 11,183 round trips. It ran the account down past 2% of its starting size by early September, so the last month of the range never even got tested. The same rules on 15 minute candles paid $39,360 and kept 147%.

So the execution bill isnt a detail you tack on at the end, its the entire difference between those first two rows. A 2x ATR target on a 5 minute NQ candle is a handful of points, and a couple of ticks of friction takes a real share of that. The same 2x ATR on 15 minute candles is a much bigger target sitting on top of the same $5 round trip.

The drawdowns dont sort in the same order as the returns either. 15 minute made the most and drew down 43.2%, while 30 minute made 114.7% at 33.0%. On a prop account with a trailing drawdown, the 30 minute row is the only one of the four that gets through the rulebook.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The cost breakdown is the useful part: a +12.7% gross result turning into -99.2% net on the 5-minute version shows the edge per trade is smaller than the friction there. I'd add the average net P&L per trade in ticks for each timeframe, which makes the cost-to-edge ratio visible at a glance, and a sensitivity run with slippage at one tick and zero to see where each row breaks even. Since the 15-, 30- and 60-minute rows share the same trending stretches, the independent sample is smaller than the trade counts suggest. News days (CPI, FOMC, NFP) also dominate NQ's average ranges, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for checking how much of the profit sits on those days.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Those are fair additions. Average net P&L per trade in ticks plus zero, half and one tick slippage would show the break-even friction directly instead of leaving readers to infer it from net return.

The independence point matters just as much. Four rows do not create four separate market histories, because they share the same NQ trends. I'd split each timeframe into identical non-overlapping calendar blocks, then tag CPI, FOMC and NFP windows separately. That would show whether the 15 and 30 minute results persist across regimes or are being carried by the same handful of macro moves.
